questions.title: Java Records (Java 16+)
questions.question: What are Java Records, when should you use them, and what are their limitations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Record: concise immutable data carrier class — auto-generates constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString
- Fields are final by default — records are immutable
- Cannot extend another class (implicitly extends Record); can implement interfaces
- Can have compact constructor for validation
- Use cases: DTOs, value objects, API request/response models, configuration holders
- Limitations: no mutable fields, no inheritance, no JPA @Entity (no default no-arg constructor)
- Records with Jackson: works out of the box in Jackson 2.12+

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Records are a concise way to declare immutable data classes. In a single line you declare the type and its fields, and Java generates the canonical constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode, and toString automatically. This eliminates the boilerplate that previously required either Lombok or many manual lines of code.

The best use cases are DTOs, API request and response models, value objects, and any data that you just want to hold and pass around without modification. A record with user ID, name, and email is a perfect fit — you create it once with all its data and pass it around.

The key limitation is immutability — you can't have mutable fields in a record, which is intentional. You also can't use a record as a JPA entity because JPA requires a no-argument constructor and mutable fields. Records also can't extend classes, though they can implement interfaces.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Records are a concise way to declare immutable data classes.
speakable_v2.cap: Records also can't extend classes, though they can implement interfaces.

questions.title: Sealed Classes and Pattern Matching
questions.question: What are sealed classes and pattern matching in Java, and how do they improve domain modeling?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Sealed class/interface: restricts which classes can extend/implement it
- permits clause: explicitly lists allowed subtypes
- Works with pattern matching switch: exhaustive — compiler ensures all cases handled
- Pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+): if (obj instanceof String s) — avoids cast
- switch expressions with pattern matching (Java 21): concise and exhaustive switching
- Use case: closed type hierarchies like Result<T>, event types, payment methods — ADTs
- Deconstructor patterns (Java 21): switch with record patterns

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them. Instead of any class anywhere being able to extend your base class, you explicitly declare the permitted subtypes with the permits clause. This gives you a closed type hierarchy — the compiler knows all possible subtypes.

The power of sealed classes comes with pattern matching in switch expressions. Because the compiler knows all permitted subtypes, it can verify that your switch is exhaustive — you've handled every possible case. If you add a new permitted subtype later, every switch that handles the sealed type becomes a compile error until you add the new case. This makes your code much more maintainable.

The classic use case is a Result type — either a Success with a value or a Failure with an error. Sealed classes model this perfectly. Every caller switches on the result and must handle both cases — the compiler won't let them forget the error case.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Every caller switches on the result and must handle both cases — the compiler won't let them forget the error case.

questions.title: Text Blocks and String Features
questions.question: What are Java text blocks and what other modern String features should you know?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Text block (Java 15+): multi-line string literal with triple quotes
- Automatic stripping of incidental whitespace based on closing delimiter indent
- Useful for: SQL, JSON, HTML, XML, GraphQL in Java code
- Escape sequences: \s preserves trailing whitespace; \ continues line without newline
- String methods: isBlank(), strip(), stripLeading(), stripTrailing(), repeat(), lines()
- String.formatted(): inline String.format() alternative
- stripIndent() and translateEscapes() for dynamic text blocks

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Text blocks solve the multi-line string problem. Before Java 15, embedding multi-line SQL or JSON in Java required escaping quotes and joining lines with backslash-n, making the code hard to read. Text blocks use triple quotes and preserve the natural indentation without requiring escape characters.

The incidental whitespace stripping is clever — the closing triple-quote's position determines how much leading whitespace is stripped from all lines. If the closing quote is at column 8, it strips 8 spaces of indentation from every line, making the string content align as intended in the source code.

For Spring Data repositories, text blocks make complex native queries much more readable. A multi-line SQL with CTEs and multiple joins can be written exactly as you'd write it in a SQL editor, embedded directly in the Java annotation.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Text blocks solve the multi-line string problem.
speakable_v2.cap: A multi-line SQL with CTEs and multiple joins can be written exactly as you'd write it in a SQL editor, embedded directly in the Java annotation.

questions.title: Switch Expressions and Enhanced Switch
questions.question: How do switch expressions differ from switch statements in Java, and what patterns can you use?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Switch expression (Java 14+): produces a value, arrow syntax (->), no fall-through
- yield: return value from a block in switch expression
- No fall-through: arrow case handles one label without break needed
- Multiple labels: case A, B, C -> ... instead of separate cases with fall-through
- Pattern matching in switch (Java 21): instanceof pattern, guards with 'when'
- Exhaustiveness: switch expressions require all cases covered (or default)
- Prefer switch expressions over statements for concise conditional value assignment

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Switch expressions, introduced in Java 14, can return a value and have a much cleaner syntax. The arrow case eliminates fall-through — each case handles its own result independently. This eliminates a whole class of bugs where developers forget to add a break statement.

For assigning a value based on a condition, switch expressions are far cleaner than if-else chains or the old switch statement with break on every case. You can use it directly in an assignment, in a return statement, or as a method argument.

With Java 21's pattern matching, switch becomes extremely powerful. You can match on the type of an object, destructure records in case patterns, and add guard conditions with when. Combined with sealed classes, the compiler ensures exhaustiveness — you can't forget a case.

questions.title: Optional — Proper Usage and Anti-Patterns
questions.question: How should you use Optional in Java and what are the common anti-patterns to avoid?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Optional: container that may or may not contain a value — makes null absence explicit in API
- Don't use Optional as method parameter or field — use for return types only
- Don't use Optional.get() without isPresent() check — defeats the purpose
- orElse() vs orElseGet(): orElse always evaluates the argument; orElseGet is lazy
- orElseThrow(): clean alternative to explicit null check + throw
- map/flatMap/filter: chain transformations without null checks
- Stream.ofNullable: bridge between nullable values and streams

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Optional is a return type signal that says 'this method might not return a value.' It forces callers to explicitly handle the absence case, making null-pointer risks visible at the API boundary. The key rule is to only use Optional as a return type — not as a field, method parameter, or constructor argument.

The most common mistake is using Optional.get() without first checking isPresent(), which throws NoSuchElementException and defeats the purpose. The better pattern is to use orElse for a default value, orElseGet for a lazy default, orElseThrow to throw a meaningful exception, or map/flatMap to chain transformations without touching the value directly.

The difference between orElse and orElseGet matters when the default is expensive to compute. orElse always evaluates its argument — if you pass a method call, that method runs even when the Optional has a value. orElseGet takes a Supplier that only runs when the Optional is empty.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Optional is a return type signal that says 'this method might not return a value.' It forces callers to explicitly handle the absence case, making null-pointer risks visible at the API boundary.
speakable_v2.cap: orElseGet takes a Supplier that only runs when the Optional is empty.

questions.title: Functional Interfaces and Lambda Expressions
questions.question: What are functional interfaces and how do lambdas and method references work in Java?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Functional interface: exactly one abstract method — @FunctionalInterface annotation
- Built-in: Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>, Supplier<T>, Consumer<T>, BiFunction<T,U,R>
- Lambda: concise anonymous implementation of a functional interface
- Method reference: shorthand for lambda that just calls an existing method
- Closure: lambda captures effectively final local variables
- Composition: Function.andThen(), Predicate.and()/or()/negate()
- Custom functional interfaces: when built-ins don't fit (e.g., checked exceptions)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method. Lambdas are concise implementations of functional interfaces — wherever a functional interface is expected, you can pass a lambda expression or a method reference instead of an anonymous class. Java's built-in functional interfaces cover most scenarios: Function transforms a value, Predicate tests a condition, Supplier produces a value, and Consumer processes a value.

Method references are shorthand for lambdas that simply delegate to an existing method. Instead of x -> x.toString(), you write Object::toString. Instead of x -> new User(x), you write User::new. They're more readable when the lambda body is just a single method call.

Composing functional interfaces is where they become really powerful. You chain Predicates with and, or, negate to build complex filtering conditions without nested if statements. You chain Functions with andThen to build transformation pipelines. This is the foundation of the Stream API.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This is the foundation of the Stream API.
